content: Gardnerella vaginalis is a bacterial species belonging to the genus Gardnerella, which is classified as gram-variable. It is the sole species within this genus and is known to cause bacterial vaginosis in certain women. Gardnerella vaginalis, previously referred to as Haemophilus vaginalis and Corynebacterium vaginale, is a facultative anaerobic, non-motile, pleomorphic rod-shaped bacterium. It exhibits gram-negative to gram-variable staining characteristics. This organism is a recognized colonizer of the female genital tract and thrives in environments with a high pH. However, it demonstrates poor survival in human urine at 37°C. The bacterium was first identified by Leopold and later named Haemophilus vaginalis by Gardner and Dukes in 1955, as it was initially isolated using human blood bilayer agar media. This method yielded limited bacterial growth, leading to the development of alternative media such as HBT (with Tween 80) and HB (without Tween 80). HB medium consists of a basal layer of Columbia agar base with colistin, nalidixic acid, and amphotericin B, overlaid with the same composition plus 5% human blood. HBT agar includes Proteose Peptone No. 3 and Tween 80 in both the basal and overlay layers. These media enhance the production of human blood hemolysis by G. vaginalis, facilitating its detection even in the presence of other vaginal flora. G. vaginalis is resistant to lactobacilli and several antibiotics, including tetracycline. Genome sequencing is crucial to understanding its resistance mechanisms and identifying the genes responsible for its ability to adhere to epithelial cells and proliferate despite the presence of probiotics and antibiotics. The genome is approximately 0.72 Mb in size with a GC content of 42-44%. Research on this bacterium has been limited due to challenges in lysing the microbe. No plasmids have been identified yet, but DNA isolation techniques may enable further exploration of chromosomal DNA and potential extrachromosomal plasmids. Gardnerella vaginalis is gram-variable, displaying characteristics of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. During exponential growth, it may appear gram-positive, but as it ages, the peptidoglycan layer becomes too thin to retain crystal violet-iodine complexes, resulting in a gram-negative appearance. The bacterium is surrounded by an exopolysaccharide layer and pili, which facilitate adherence to vaginal epithelial cells. Its cell wall contains straight-chain saturated and unsaturated non-hydroxylated fatty acids, including hexadecanoic acid and octadecenoic acid, along with significant amounts of alanine, glycine, glutamic acid, and lysine. G. vaginalis exhibits a complex metabolism and is a facultative anaerobe, capable of metabolizing glucose and other simple sugars under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. In both metabolic states, it produces lactic acid as a byproduct. Gardnerella vaginalis is one of the few microorganisms consistently associated with bacterial vaginosis in women. It is found in humans and some animals, such as mares and horses. Apart from the urinary tract and bladder, it can also colonize the endometrium, fetal membranes, and newborn infants, often resulting from maternal or neonatal infections and suppurative lesions. The bacterium can also be transmitted through sexual intercourse. G. vaginalis adheres more effectively to urogenital squamous epithelial cells due to its exopolysaccharide layer and pili. It forms biofilms that are resistant to antibiotic treatment and induce inflammatory processes, displacing indigenous lactobacilli from their habitat. This attachment allows the bacterium to migrate from the genitourinary tract to its primary colonization site in the bladder. Women, who have squamous cells in their genitourinary tract and bladder, are more susceptible to this pathogen compared to men, whose bladders lack these cells. In women affected by G. vaginalis, clue cell-like squamous epithelial cells can be observed in bladder urine obtained via suprapubic aspiration, whereas no such cells are observed in men. Despite its clinical significance, little is known about the pathogenic mechanisms of G. vaginalis. The bacterium secretes a 60-kDa hemolysin that lyses human erythrocytes, neutrophils, and endothelial cells, making it a potential virulence factor. Symptoms of bacterial vaginosis caused by G. vaginalis in women may include gray, foul-smelling vaginal discharge (with a fishy odor particularly noticeable after intercourse due to the alkaline nature of semen reacting with the bacteria), vaginal itching or burning, discomfort during urination, and pain during sexual intercourse. Men typically do not exhibit physical symptoms. Infections with G. vaginalis are associated with proteolysis, leading to the production of nitrogenous compounds such as cadaverine and putrescine, which contribute to a bad odor and water loss.
